points: A cache keeps a copy of data closer to the reader than the source of truth, so most reads skip the slow path.
The price is staleness: every write must reach the cache too, and races with invalidations can leave it holding a value the database no longer has.
Uber built its cache inside the database and used the database's own change log as the signal to invalidate entries.
Meta counts only inconsistencies a client could actually observe, and its checker caught a rare bug in an error-handling path.

figures.label: over 10 trillion cache fills per day, even at a 99% hit rate
99.99% of cached reads matched the database in compare mode

prerequisiteReasons.load-balancing: Caching takes from load balancing the picture of requests spread across a pool of servers, and of some server in the path answering instead of the origin.

points: Consensus is how a group of replicas agree on one value, or one order of values, even though machines crash and messages are lost.
A leader appends each change to a replicated log, and a change counts as committed once a majority has stored it.
Any two majorities overlap, so a minority of nodes can fail and the system still agrees; the cost is a majority round trip on every write.
The etcd guide says commit latency has a floor set by the network round trip between members plus a durable disk write.

figures.label: member round trip: about 50 ms in the US, up to 400 ms intercontinental
lease-maintenance CPU use cut by up to 85% with Leader Leases

prerequisiteReasons.cap: Consensus takes from CAP the choice of strong consistency, and the cost that the system keeps serving only while a quorum of nodes survives.
prerequisiteReasons.replication: Consensus takes from replication the picture of several copies of the same data, which must all apply the same changes in the same order.
